worksheets.title: Data Collection, Summary Statistics and Outliers

fluency_questions.prompt: For the $5$ ordered data scores $4, 6, 6, 8, 11$, find:

parts.label: a
parts.question: The mode (most common score)

parts.label: b
parts.question: The range ($\text{highest} - \text{lowest} = 11 - 4$)

parts.label: c
parts.question: The median (the middle score)

parts.label: d
parts.question: The mean ($\text{sum} \div 5 = 35 \div 5$)

fluency_questions.prompt: First organise the $5$ scores $10, 3, 7, 3, 12$ into ascending order ($3, 3, 7, 10, 12$), then find:

parts.label: a
parts.question: The mode

parts.label: b
parts.question: The range ($12 - 3$)

parts.label: c
parts.question: The median (middle score)

parts.label: d
parts.question: The mean ($35 \div 5$)

parts.label: a
parts.question: The range ($12 - 2$)

parts.label: b
parts.question: The two middle scores

parts.label: c
parts.question: The median (halfway between $6$ and $8$: $\frac{6 + 8}{2}$)

parts.label: d
parts.question: The mean ($42 \div 6$)

fluency_questions.prompt: State whether each survey is a **Census** (whole population) or a **Sample** (part of the population):

parts.label: a
parts.question: Surveying every student in your Year 8 homeroom about homeroom seating

parts.label: b
parts.question: Surveying $50$ shoppers at Chadstone about Victorian shopping habits

parts.label: c
parts.question: The Australian Government counting every household in Australia

parts.label: d
parts.question: Testing $10$ apples from an orchard of $5000$ trees for sweetness

application_questions.question: Over $5$ autumn days in Hobart, the maximum temperatures were $14^\circ\text{C}, 16^\circ\text{C}, 16^\circ\text{C}, 18^\circ\text{C}$, and $21^\circ\text{C}$. Add the $5$ temperatures and divide by $5$ to find the mean temperature.
Five players in an AFLW match kicked $1, 2, 2, 3$, and $12$ behinds. Identify the **outlier** (the extreme score far from the others) and find the median of the $5$ scores.
Aria scored $7, 8$, and $9$ on three spelling quizzes (mean $= 8$). If she scores $12$ on the fourth quiz, calculate $\dfrac{7 + 8 + 9 + 12}{4}$ to find her new mean.
A stem-and-leaf plot of $5$ test marks (where $2 \mid 3 = 23$) has ordered scores $18, 21, 23, 25, 43$. Find the median (middle score) and the range ($43 - 18$).

reasoning_questions.question: To find the median of $8, 2, 10, 4, 5$, Ben picks the middle number in the list and says the median is $10$. Explain what Ben forgot to do first and find the correct median.
reasoning_questions.answer: Ben forgot to put the scores in ascending order first ($2, 4, 5, 8, 10$). The middle score of the ordered list is $5$.

reasoning_questions.question: In the house prices $\$500\text{k}, \$520\text{k}, \$530\text{k}, \$550\text{k}, \$2\,900\text{k}$, explain why the **median** ($\$530\text{k}$) describes a typical house better than the **mean** ($\$1\,000\text{k}$).
reasoning_questions.answer: The extreme outlier ($\$2\,900\text{k}$) pulls the mean up to $\$1\,000\text{k}$ (higher than $4$ of the $5$ houses), whereas the median is not affected by the outlier.

worksheets.title: Sampling Methods, Data Displays, and Comparing Distributions

fluency_questions.prompt: Match each survey description to **Random sample** (fair) or **Biased sample** (unfair):

parts.label: a
parts.question: Drawing $30$ student names out of a hat containing all Year 8 students

parts.label: b
parts.question: Asking only the students on the soccer team what their favourite sport is

parts.label: c
parts.question: Using a computer random number generator to pick $50$ electoral roll voters

parts.label: d
parts.question: Surveying only your $4$ best friends about school uniform rules

fluency_questions.prompt: A stem-and-leaf plot of $7$ test scores (where $3 \mid 2 = 32$) shows: $2 \mid 5, 8$; $3 \mid 0, 2, 6$; $4 \mid 1, 5$. Find:

parts.label: a
parts.question: The lowest score ($2 \mid 5$)

parts.label: b
parts.question: The highest score ($4 \mid 5$)

parts.label: c
parts.question: The range ($45 - 25$)

parts.label: d
parts.question: The median (the $4$th score in order)

fluency_questions.prompt: Identify the shape of each graph from the list: **Symmetric**, **Positively skewed** (tail to the right), **Negatively skewed** (tail to the left):

parts.label: a
parts.question: Left side and right side are mirror images around the middle peak

parts.label: b
parts.question: Tall bars on the left with a long tail stretching to the right

parts.label: c
parts.question: Tall bars on the right with a long tail stretching to the left

parts.label: d
parts.question: In a symmetric distribution, are the mean and median approximately equal?

fluency_questions.prompt: Compare the $5$ ordered scores of Team A ($10, 12, 14, 16, 18$) and Team B ($6, 10, 14, 18, 22$):

parts.label: a
parts.question: Find the median (middle score) of Team A and Team B

parts.label: b
parts.question: Find the range of Team A ($18 - 10$)

parts.label: c
parts.question: Find the range of Team B ($22 - 6$)

parts.label: d
parts.question: Which team has more consistent (less spread out) scores?

application_questions.question: A school has $200$ Year 7 students and $300$ Year 8 students ($500$ in total). If $10\%$ of each year level is chosen for a survey, calculate $10\%$ of $200$ and $10\%$ of $300$ to find how many students are chosen from each year.

Over $5$ games, Mia's basketball scores have median $18$ and range $6$, while Zoe's scores have median $15$ and range $14$. Who has the higher typical score (median), and who is more consistent (smaller range)?
application_questions.answer: Mia has both the higher typical score ($18 > 15$) and is more consistent (range $6 < 14$).

application_questions.question: A dot plot of the number of pets owned by $15$ families in Ballarat has most dots at $0, 1, 2$ pets and one dot at $9$ pets (a hobby farm). Is this distribution positively skewed (tail to the right) or negatively skewed?
application_questions.answer: Positively skewed (the tail stretches to the high value $9$ on the right).

application_questions.question: A radio station asks listeners to phone in and pay $\$1$ to vote on a new road toll. Explain in one sentence why this sample is biased.
application_questions.answer: Only listeners who feel strongly enough to phone in and pay $\$1$ will vote (self-selection bias), leaving out everyone else.

reasoning_questions.question: Why is it much faster and cheaper to survey a random **sample** of $1000$ Australians about television habits rather than conducting a **census** of all $27\text{ million}$ Australians?
reasoning_questions.answer: Contacting all $27\text{ million}$ people takes huge time and cost, whereas a well-chosen random sample of $1000$ people gives an accurate estimate quickly and cheaply.

reasoning_questions.question: In Question 4, Team A and Team B both have a median of $14$ and a mean of $14$. Explain why we also need to calculate the **range** to tell the two teams apart.
reasoning_questions.answer: The median and mean only tell us the middle/average score; the range shows that Team B's scores are twice as spread out ($16$ vs $8$) as Team A's.
